I'm maintaining a couple personal pet projects and I've recently noticed in google search console that on both projects impressions and clicks went from 500-700 impressions / 10-15 clicks daily to almost zero in one day. First I thought that I broke something (e.g. added noindex by mistake or so), but everything was good and content was good, fresh and up to date. I went researching and it turned out Google changed their anti-spam policy and dropped A LOT of links from their index around Oct 26 or so. From what I see is that they're trying to remove a lot of fake abusive AI-generated content from their index. I also had some nice insights and help in google community regarding my problem and they mentioned that they're cleaning stuff. In general I think it's not so bad to fight with useless AI-generated content, on the other hand my content wasn't that sloppy, it was actually quite useful (at least for me and a few readers), distilled knowledge. But it fell into that "too bad to keep it in the index" criteria :/ I'll work on my projects content, it's not a problem and I've learned the lesson. But I'm wondering how many indie hackers / builders and "SEO hackers" were affected? Many of young products depend on the search traffic so they'll be suffering because their domain / content is not trustworthy. Do you think it's a temporary measure or we'll have higher quality expectations from search engines in the future?

AI has become really good at coding in some sense, that's undeniable, and there are people that say you don't really need to review their code anymore. But I keep getting stuck in a sensation that's between cognitive dissonance, FOMO, and a vague sense of being gaslit, because when I review the code it writes - and this is all of them - 80% of it is right, and 20% is wrong, but in extremely subtle ways; only when you deeply understand the system and carefully review it do you spot the issues. These are not stylistic choices, the code is incorrect. Of course, the AI fixes it when you prompt it to, but you need to work very hard to know what needs prompting. This is all after the grill-me skills and cross-model adversarial review and whatnot (all these techniques do help somewhat but they didn't get it perfect), For example, I had AI (Opus 5.5 and Gemini both tried, in this particular case) write an integration test for our system, to reproduce an issue we had. It failed because it chose, for simplicity, to combine two backend fakes into one store, having writes covered by the same mutex, but the bug was only happening in production when these two stores went out of sync (and they did because we wrote to both concurrently and one write failed). (I don't want to argue the merits of the design. This is existing code.) The wrong code it wrote to try and find the issue was carefully written, well organized, function names were reasonable, etc. etc. I can't be alone in this, but I can't put my finger on what exactly goes wrong in the process. Can you share examples of changes you wanted to make that Claude and the bunch (frontier versions) got subtly wrong?

In this spring and early/mid summer, we saw tons of headlines about how "programming/coding/software has changed forever", and now, suddenly, we see very similar headlines about math, some from very prominent mathematicians. To those of HNers well versed in both, which disruption do you think has been bigger `so far`, if any at all? Thanks

In math there are more obvious examples of AI achieving things that humans have failed to achieve for decades without AI. But in practice the number of mathematicians is relatively tiny and most of the value they produce economically isn't tied to how many cutting edge proofs they produce. So the changes are massively disrupting but not as existential as they feel to some of the mathematicians - they'll still be able to do research, write papers, teach, give talks and everything else they've been doing; the changes will be in the tools available, ways of working and in the system of incentives in academia which will finally be forced to stop pretending that people's value comes from publishing papers (it was never true but the people who are most upset now are the ones who fell for that lie).

But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052 ). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ( https://regressions.net ). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything. The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai . We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now. If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

Digging under the hood, hey there's a Linux VM and a Chrome browser. This is really cool because it essentially defines an environment that is really similar to a typical workstation. After some playing around I got the LimaCharlie EDR installed, the Chrome LC EDR installed and the email provider connected to the LC Email Security. Took a few iteration to make it all smooth but it works great on the free community edition! So you get to see what is executing on the box, where the bot is browsing and emails in and out. I built a couple detections using AI and just made it a doc in our documentation so you can just tell Grok Bot: """ Secure my Grok Bot with LimaCharlie by following https://docs.limacharlie.io/grok-bot/ """ The TL;DR; of what it does: - all of it goes to your own private tenant - installs a linux EDR on the box - installs a Chrome extension that is essentially an EDR in your browser - if you want, connects your gmail (any IMAP is supported really) and is like an EDR for the email - If you want it sends the alerts to your Grok Bot (I'm curious to see the advantage of a feedback loop here), or it's available on the web app.limacharlie.io The other option I left in was to leave the CLI authenticated on the Grok Bot. The interesting bit about that is that because the CLI has 100% coverage of the platform, you can ask the Grok Bot to start setting up new alerts, investigate alerts, configure everything... I tried to make it more generic for other AI agents where I have no idea what the environment is: https://docs.limacharlie.io/2-sensors-deployment/tutorials/s... though disclaimer I have not tried it yet, but it's not rocket science and more frontier AI models are now rocket scientists. The advantage that Grok Bot has is that it fundamentally allows things to execute on the VM and talk out. The other ones (Muse, Dots) seem to proxy every single thing and generally be extremely difficult to extend. Anyway, hope it helps some of you! (and yes, got it to make a cool video :D) https://youtu.be/yZZuBgKWd1k
